newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN POLICE BATTLE TO GET FINANCIAL CONTROL.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN POLICE BATTLE TO GET FINANCIAL CONTROL.

text.p: The South African Police Service's awesome task of tackling the country's rapidly escalating crime rate is matched almost by the nightmare of ensuring proper financial control in the formerly fragmented force.

The problem, Commissioner George Fivaz told the parliamentary public accounts committee on Wednesday, was that the force was still grappling with the problem of amalgamating the former 11 police forces from South Africa and the so-called black "homelands" after the country's first democratic elections in 1994.

During the force's annual grilling on the Auditor-General's report on its budget, Fivaz said he hoped to have most of the debris of amalgamation cleared away by the end of this year with the help of newly appointed chief executive officer, South Africa Breweries chairman Meyer Khan.

After three hours of intense questioning by the committee, it was clear the SAPS was not only short of skilled staff in critical areas such as information technology, but it had inherited weak administrative systems in every area from pay and leave records to purchases of fuel and uniforms.

The situation was not helped by the fact that most records, especially from the former homelands, were in a poor state and had to be checked manually. This was particularly arduous when it came to checking the leave and promotion records of the 140,000 members of the force.

While the police were tasked with rooting out crime and corruption in South Africa at large, the committee heard that they were not above indulging in some themselves to compensate for stress and poor working conditions.
For example, Fivaz admitted, some members had taken to using so-called sick leave as a form of industrial action.
"I believe it is called Blue Flu," he said.

Committee members expressed concern about the fact that medical aid contributions paid out by the police medical aid had jumped by 34 percent in 1995/96 to about one billion rand. Khan said this was partly due to the increase in the number of members in the new integrated force.
"But it is also because of the abuse, the mismanagement and the fraud related to the fund," he said, adding that the situation had been exacerbated by the fact that the fund offered fixed benefits.
Khan, who has been in office for a week at the behest of President Nelson Mandela to sort out the police force, was unfazed by all these problems.
"I have been a policeman for a week now and have enjoyed it thoroughly," he told Reuters.
"We are going to prioritise the problems, find out which the important ones are, and we are going to sort them out."
